claims.text: Boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment currently have limited resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion.
A thin chromium coating will improve the molten-aluminum corrosion resistance of boride-based components.
PVD or sputtering can be used to deposit the proposed chromium-containing surface coating.
Thermal activation of the chromium coating at 660–700°C will form a stable protective phase.
Thermal activation will produce a continuous chromium-rich intermetallic or oxide layer at the coating–boride interface.
At high temperature, the chromium coating will diffuse and react to form the proposed barrier.
The chromium-rich barrier will limit diffusion of aluminum into the boride substrate.
Limiting aluminum diffusion into the substrate will reduce interfacial degradation and corrosion.
Chromium-coated samples will have lower corrosion depth than uncoated boride samples.
Chromium-coated samples will have lower corrosion current density than uncoated boride samples.
The chromium coating may reduce corrosion depth and corrosion current density by at least 30–50%.
The appropriate experimental baseline is an otherwise identical boride-based component without chromium surface treatment.
The coating will remain effective under standard hot-dip aluminum-plating conditions of 660–700°C and typical exposure durations.
Substantially higher temperatures or prolonged exposure may destabilize the protective layer and reduce its effectiveness.
Coated and uncoated samples will be exposed to molten aluminum at the same temperature and for the same duration.
Cross-sectional microscopy, electrochemical testing, SEM, and XRD will assess corrosion depth, corrosion current density, integrity, and phase formation.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant 30–50% reduction in corrosion depth and/or corrosion current density will falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The target is expressed ambiguously as 'at least 30–50%,' while the falsification rule treats 'less than a 30–50% reduction' as a single threshold. It also equates failure of statistical significance with failure to reach an effect-size threshold, although these are not equivalent criteria.
